props.title: The Last Mistress
props.initialSlug: Dangerous affair tests aristocrat's arranged marriage

sections.content: The Last Mistress (2007) marks a pivotal moment in French provocateur Catherine Breillat's career, merging her signature sexual frankness with period drama sophistication. Like her earlier Romance (1999) and Anatomy of Hell (2004), it fearlessly explores female sexuality, but here wraps it in sumptuous 19th-century costumes and settings. Asia Argento's volcanic performance as Vellini, a Spanish courtesan who refuses to release her grip on a young aristocrat, channels the raw carnality of Betty Blue (1986) while adding layers of psychological complexity.

sections.content: Breillat's film sits within a rich tradition of French period eroticism, including Dangerous Beauty (1998) and Quills (2000), but subverts the typical costume drama's polite restraint. The film's extended flashback structure, revealing the decade-long affair between Vellini and Ryno de Marigny, creates a fascinating tension between past passion and present propriety. This narrative approach echoes The Age of Innocence (1993), though Breillat's treatment is far more explicit in its exploration of obsessive desire.

The film's visual style merges the painterly composition of Barry Lyndon (1975) with the intimate immediacy of In the Realm of the Senses (1976). Cinematographer Yorgos Arvanitis creates candlelit scenes that reference Caravaggio while maintaining a raw, almost documentary-like quality during the film's more intimate moments. This technical achievement supports Breillat's broader mission of demystifying sexuality while examining its role in power dynamics and personal identity. SUBHEAD: Breaking Period Drama Conventions

sections.content: Where most costume dramas like The Piano (1993) or Portrait of a Lady (1996) sublimate desire beneath layers of propriety, The Last Mistress strips away these pretenses. Breillat's approach influenced later works like Lady Macbeth (2016) and The Favourite (2018), which similarly challenge the genre's traditional restraint. The film's frank treatment of sexuality and power prefigures contemporary period pieces like Portrait of a Lady on Fire (2019), demonstrating how historical settings can illuminate modern sexual politics.
